notes_sections.title: Core Advanced Concepts
notes_sections.content: At Level 3, problems include very large numbers, algebraic expressions, fractions, decimals, and complex word problems. HCF is also called GCD (Greatest Common Divisor) and LCM means Least Common Multiple. Prime factorization is the most reliable method, while Euclid’s Division Algorithm is best for large numbers.

notes_sections.title: Euclid Algorithm and Linear Representation
notes_sections.content: To find gcd(a, b), repeatedly divide the larger number by the smaller and continue with the remainder until it becomes zero. The last non-zero remainder is the GCD. Also, gcd(a, b) can be written in the form ax + by, which is useful in advanced competitive exams.

notes_sections.title: HCF and LCM of Algebraic Expressions
notes_sections.content: For algebraic terms, factor each expression completely. For HCF, take common factors with the smallest power. For LCM, take all factors with the highest power. Example: HCF of 6x²y and 9xy³ is 3xy, and LCM is 18x²y³.

notes_sections.title: LCM and HCF of Fractions and Decimals
notes_sections.content: LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators divided by HCF of denominators. HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators divided by LCM of denominators. For decimals, first convert them into whole numbers by removing decimal points.

notes_sections.title: Advanced ₹ Based Word Problems
notes_sections.content: Three machines produce goods worth ₹1500, ₹2100, and ₹3150 per cycle. To divide the total investment into equal groups, find HCF(1500, 2100, 3150) = 150. To find when all production cycles coincide, calculate their LCM.

notes_sections.title: Important Properties
notes_sections.content: If two numbers are co-prime, their HCF is 1 and LCM equals their product. If gcd(a, b) = 1, then gcd(a, bc) = gcd(a, c). These properties save time in exams.

notes_sections.title: Common Mistakes
notes_sections.content: Ignoring powers while factoring algebraic terms, applying the product formula to more than two numbers, and mixing up LCM and HCF formulas for fractions.

notes_sections.title: Quick Summary
notes_sections.content: Use Euclid’s Algorithm for large numbers, prime factorization for expressions, and special formulas for fractions. Clear understanding of properties is essential at competitive level.

tricks.title: Repeated Division Trick
tricks.explanation: Keep dividing until the remainder becomes zero. The last divisor is the GCD.

tricks.title: Fast LCM Using GCD
tricks.explanation: First find HCF, then apply LCM = (a × b) ÷ HCF.

tricks.title: Algebra Factor Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Take out common variables with smallest powers for HCF.

tricks.title: Fraction LCM Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Use numerator LCM and denominator HCF.

tricks.title: Identify Co-primes Quickly
tricks.explanation: If numbers share no common prime factors, HCF is 1.

tricks.title: Power Comparison Rule
tricks.explanation: For LCM take highest powers, for HCF take lowest powers.

tricks.title: Decimal Conversion Trick
tricks.explanation: Remove decimal points by multiplying with powers of 10.

tricks.title: Reduce Multiple Numbers
tricks.explanation: Solve in pairs step by step.

tricks.title: Option Elimination Strategy
tricks.explanation: In MCQs, eliminate options smaller than the largest given number for LCM.
tricks.example: If largest number is 40, LCM cannot be less than 40.

tricks.title: ₹ Grouping Strategy
tricks.explanation: For equal distribution problems, immediately think of HCF.
